title: How would you estimate how many cups of coffee London cafés sell on a weekday?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many cups of coffee do London cafés sell on a weekday?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: London cafés sell roughly 3.5 million cups of coffee on a typical weekday. You get there by counting the adults in London on a working day, the share who buy a café coffee, and how many cups each of them drinks, then checking the result against how many cafés there are. Try your own estimate before you read on.
body:
The question

How many cups of coffee do London cafés sell on a weekday?

This is a friendly opener. You have bought a coffee in a city, so you already have the instincts. The test is whether you can turn those instincts into a clean chain of assumptions, say each one out loud and check the answer from a second direction.

Clarify before you calculate

Spend 20 seconds pinning down the scope. Good clarifying questions here are:

  • What counts as a café? Chains, independents, sandwich shops, station kiosks and workplace cafés all make coffee to order. Supermarket meal-deal cans and office machines do not.
  • Which London? Greater London, the 32 boroughs plus the City.
  • Which unit? Cups, not dollars. If the interviewer later wants value, you multiply by an average price.

Then give a rough guess so you have something to check against: "My instinct is a few million cups a day."

Choose the approach

Use the demand side (start from buyers): adults in London on a weekday × share who buy a café coffee × cups per buyer. It is the easier side to reason about, because you can picture your own habits and those of people you know. Then use the supply side (start from outlets) as the cross-check. If you want a refresher on choosing between the two, see buyers' side versus sellers' side.

Step by step

StepAssumptionRunning total
London residentsAbout 9M9M
Adults onlyRoughly 7M of them are adults7M
Add weekday visitorsAbout 1M commuters from outside London and tourists8M
Buy a café coffee today30%8M × 30% = 2.4M buyers
Cups per buyer1.5 (some buy one, some buy two)2.4M × 1.5 = 3.6M cups

That gives about 3.6M cups on a weekday. Round it and say "roughly 3.5 million".

Why exclude children? Almost nobody under 16 buys café coffee, and including them would force you to lower the 30% to an awkward number. Stripping them out first keeps each assumption easy to defend.

Sanity check from the supply side

Now estimate the same number from the outlets. These are illustrative assumptions, not a census of London cafés:

  • Chain coffee shops: 3,000 × 400 cups a day = 1.2M
  • Independent cafés: 6,000 × 150 cups a day = 0.9M
  • Other outlets (sandwich chains, bakeries, kiosks, workplace cafés): 5,000 × 200 cups a day = 1.0M

Total: 3.1M cups. The two methods land within about 15% of each other, which is as close as you can expect. You can now say with some confidence that the answer is between 3 and 3.5 million, and that the outlet counts are the weaker link.

Which assumption matters most

Population is the easy number. Behaviour is where the uncertainty sits. Test it:

  • If 25% buy a coffee instead of 30%, the answer falls to 8M × 25% × 1.5 = 3.0M, which is 600k fewer cups.
  • If buyers average 1.3 cups instead of 1.5, it falls to 8M × 30% × 1.3 = 3.12M.

The share of people buying is the lever to name. It also changes most by location: a weekday in the City or Canary Wharf looks nothing like a residential street in outer London. If you had more time, you would segment office workers, other adults and tourists, each with their own purchase rate.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I'll size this from buyers and check it against outlets. About 8 million adults are in London on a weekday, including commuters. I'll assume 30% buy a café coffee and drink 1.5 cups each, so about 3.6 million cups. From the supply side, around 14,000 outlets selling 150 to 400 cups each gets me to about 3 million. So I'd say 3 to 3.5 million, and the share of people buying is the assumption I'd test first."

A weak answer sounds like this:

"London has 9 million people, a quarter buy coffee, 1.5 cups each, so 3.38 million."

The arithmetic is fine. The problem is that it includes children, ignores commuters, gives a falsely precise figure and never checks itself.

Common mistakes

  • Counting the wrong people. Residents are not the same as the people in London on a weekday. Commuters and tourists matter for a daytime habit.
  • Mixing products. A can from a supermarket fridge is not a café cup. Agree the definition up front.
  • Fake precision. Say "about 3.5 million", not "3,375,000".
  • No cross-check. One method can be wrong in a way you cannot see. The second method is what makes the answer believable.

Practice

1. How many café cups does London sell on a Saturday?

Show the answer

Commuters and office cafés drop out, but leisure visitors stay. Take 7M resident adults plus 0.5M visitors = 7.5M. Fewer people buy (25%) and they buy less often (1.3 cups): 7.5M × 25% × 1.3 = about 2.4M cups, roughly a third lower than a weekday.

2. What do Londoners spend on café coffee on a weekday?

Show the answer

3.6M cups × an average of $4.50 a cup = about $16M a day. Say whether $4.50 is the drink alone or includes the occasional pastry.

3. Roughly how many café coffees does London sell in a year?

Show the answer

250 working days × 3.6M = 900M, plus 115 weekend and holiday days × 2.4M = 276M. Total about 1.2B cups a year.

Where to practise next

Turn this into a single business with the revenue of one busy London coffee shop, which uses the same cups-per-outlet logic.
